newsitem.title: USA: HK activist Lee meets Albright, backs China MFN.
newsitem.headline: HK activist Lee meets Albright, backs China MFN.

text.p: Hong Kong democracy campaigner Martin Lee on Monday reaffirmed support for continued Most Favoured Nation trade status for China and urged U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to visit the British colony as it reverts to Beijing's control.
Speaking to reporters after talks with Albright, Lee complained that by eroding political and civil freedoms in Hong Kong, China was not helping the campaign for MFN renewal.

Lee also praised President Bill Clinton's decision to meet him later this week, and Albright's decision to see him on Monday, as conclusive evidence the United States "takes the human rights issues very seriously and is prepared to give recognition to the democratic leadership of Hong Kong."

Albright assured Lee of "strong U.S. support for continued full political and civil rights and the way of life of the people of Hong Kong," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said after the 40-minute meeting.
The secretary recalled that she and other U.S. officials have raised the issue of Hong Kong with Beijing and would continue to do so, he added.
Lee generally concurred with that assessment and said he was pleased with the "very warm" meeting he had with Albright.

Lee, a Hong Kong legislator and a leading pro-democracy campaigner who heads the colony's Democratic Party, is on a lobbying trip to Washington ahead of July 1, when Hong Kong reverts to China's control under the 1984 Sino-British agreement.

As the transition nears, there is rising concern in the United States as well as in Hong Kong that China is not living up to its promises to permit Hong Kong to function as it has, with considerable civil and political freedoms.
Increasing numbers of U.S. lawmakers have questioned whether MFN, which grants favourable U.S. trade benefits to countries, should be renewed for Beijing.
House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich on Sunday suggested that as a compromise, a renewal of six months, rather than one year, might be in order.
Lee said "the Democratic Party and I have always strongly supported the renewal MFN for China unconditionally."
He said he understood the anxiety and frustration of congressmen who were concerned as he was about the erosion of the rule of law and democracy in Hong Kong as China prepares to take control.
"China has not helped us win renewal ... I wish China would make it easier for us to win renewal," Lee said.
Despite U.S. support for Hong Kong, Albright at first scheduled no media access for her meeting with Lee, although aides later permitted photographers but not reporters to record the event.
Burns denied Albright was downplaying the meeting so as not to offend China, with whom the United States has been trying to improve relations after a seriously rocky patch.
"If the secretary was afraid of Chinese reaction, she wouldn't be meeting with Martin Lee. But the fact is she is ... We're welcoming him to Washington," he said.
